headline: Tim Waterer targets $4,500 spot gold in the near term, citing USD weakness and geopolitical tailwinds
reasoning: Waterer notes gold had been rangebound between $3,950 and $4,200 for months but broke out to around $4,400 following currency intervention that weakened the USD. He sees $4,500 as a viable short-term target, potentially achievable within the week, contingent on the dollar index sustaining a move below 100. The key downside risk to the bullish case is oil rising sharply, which could reignite inflation and interest rate hike fears.
quote: It was really stuck in a range there between, say, 3950 and 4200 for a number of months. It really couldn't get out of its own way there for a while. But that intervention we discussed, that gave it an impetus to move beyond that range to spot gold around 4400 at the moment. So looking quite positive at the moment, I think 4500. That's a viable short term target potentially even this week. I think for that to occur we need that dollar index probably to have an extended stay below the $100 level. And our oil price is not correct, too much higher. I think that is the short term risk for gold's bullish case. As if oil prices kept moving higher, that could bring inflation and interest rate hike fears back to the fall.
episode_title: Why gold could be heading for $4,500

headline: Tim Waterer sees Fed on hold or cutting in 2025 as softer US data reduces September hike probability
reasoning: Waterer notes that softer US data — including a negative jobs figure, tame CPI and PPI, and weak retail sales — has reduced the relevance of the FOMC minutes and lowered the bar for a September rate hike. He argues October is also problematic as it falls before US midterm elections, which could draw presidential ire toward Fed Chair Kevin Warsh. As a result, Waterer sees a credible path where the Fed ends the year without hiking, and potentially even cuts.
quote: I think you could also probably make the case that we could even. Yeah. Or even the fed. Yeah. Either a cut or staying on hold for this year. I think that's a very possible path for the fed. If you look at where we stand right now, we should say September looking unlikely based on recent data. October if they were to hike then that would be just before the US midterm elections. That could earn the ire of the US president for Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh there. So they could opt to pause again then, and maybe that'll give more time for data to soften further. And yes, I could well see we could get to the end of the year with no cut happening.

headline: Tim Waterer believes RBA Governor Bullock is jawboning on rate hike risk rather than signalling an imminent hike
reasoning: Waterer comes down on the side of the RBA jawboning rather than genuinely signalling a near-term hike, pointing to the improving inflation trend. Inflation has moved from a four-handle to a three-handle, which he believes the RBA is broadly satisfied with compared to the situation three months ago. However, oil price uncertainty remains a wildcard that could affect the inflation trajectory. Waterer believes Bullock is keeping the hike risk on the table mainly to temper market enthusiasm and avoid re-igniting inflationary pressures through excessive optimism.
quote: I would probably come down the side of jaw boning right now just looking at the trend of where inflation is moving. So I think the RBA will be pretty happy with sort of where it stands now once again, compared to about three months ago with inflation. More on a three handle, not a four handle. So we don't know whether that trend will be maintained or not. And I guess that ties into what happens with oil prices from here, which no one can really predict. So yes, I think she's keeping that that risk there on the table just to, I guess, keep a lid on enthusiasm a little bit and not get the market too optimistic, which could re inflate those inflationary pressures.

headline: Tim Waterer views dips in chipmakers as buying opportunities given healthy multi-year order books
reasoning: Waterer argues the semiconductor cycle is more durable this time around because contracts being locked in are of a 5 to 10 year nature rather than the one-year contracts typical in prior cycles. This extends the health of order books well into next year and beyond. The primary risk for chipmakers is not demand but factory throughput — whether they can manufacture products fast enough to meet orders. Given this dynamic, dips such as those seen in July are likely buying opportunities.
quote: I think the difference this time around is that we could be at the peak for longer. And there's a the main reason for that is I think that a lot of the, the contracts that are being locked in now, there are more of a 5 or 10 year nature rather than one year as was the case previously. So that could extend the the moves or the order book Healthiness that we're seeing at the moment. So I think right now, if you look at the revenue for the chipmakers, that the risk is not all about risk is factory throughput. Can they can they make their products, you know, quick enough? So I think with those order books looking healthy next year, year after then, I think yes, I think any dips that we have seen, such as July, will be probably buying opportunities.

headline: Tim Waterer sees AUD supported around 0.70 with potential to reach 0.735 if Fed stays on hold
reasoning: Waterer argues the Australian dollar has benefited from Japan and US intervention that depreciated the USD, providing a cushion around the 70 cent level. He sees resistance around 72.50 cents but believes if broken, the AUD could reach 73.5 cents. A Fed on-hold scenario would preserve the yield differential and further support the trade-weighted AUD.
quote: The Australian dollar it it has benefited from the moves by Japan and the US to boost the in and depreciate the US dollar. So that gave the Australian dollar a bit of a cushion around that 70% level. So if we did see further intervention down the track then that could support the Australian dollar as well. There is some resistance hanging around that 7250 mark. So I think that could be a little bit of a burden for the Aussie to try and push through. But if it did manage to get there, I think we could be looking at, you know, 73.5 cents, for example, for the Aussie, particularly if we do have that situation, we discussed where the fed does stay on hold.

headline: Tim Waterer sees Australian consumer sentiment improving as RBA pauses, but tight jobs market remains an inflation risk
reasoning: Consumer sentiment has improved from a few months ago now that RBA rate hike expectations have moderated, providing some relief to the retail market. However, the jobs market remains very tight, which Waterer identifies as a pocket of ongoing inflation risk. With unemployment at around 4.4%, Waterer believes the RBA would want to see the rate move to 4.5–4.6% to remove the inflation risk from a tight labour market. Thursday's jobs figures are notoriously difficult to predict and could shift the outlook.
quote: I think on the consumer sentiment side, I think it's a better place now than it was a few months ago. Now it looks like the RBA has put the brakes on for the moment, whereas if we wind back, say 2 or 3 months, that wasn't necessarily the case and more hikes were predicted in the short term. So I think the retail market is taking some heart from that. Jobs market is still very tight I think. So that is a pocket of inflation moving forward. So right now we're about 4.4%. Let's see how Thursday's figures pan out. They are notoriously difficult to predict the other jobs figures, so they can be quite different from what what is forecast. But I think the RBA, if they're wanting to get more of a handle on the inflation side of things, is they probably want to see that unemployment rate probably moving 4.5 4.6% just to remove that, that risk of inflation emerging from that tight jobs market.

headline: Tim Waterer flags oil as the key rogue inflation risk, with $100/bbl a threat to risk assets if sustained
reasoning: Waterer identifies oil as a structural rather than demand-side problem that central banks cannot easily address through rate policy. With the Middle East conflict ongoing since February, he sees hope for a deal as the main thing preventing oil returning to $100. If oil were to revisit and hold at that level, he believes it would pose a meaningful risk to risk assets and reignite inflation and rate-hike fears.
quote: Oil price is very much the rogue element for central banks out of their control. I think they may argue that if they were to tighten policy, that sort of addressing a demand side issue, whereas the oil is a structural problem for markets at the moment. So yes, if no deal emerges, we could see oil heading higher. And I think markets are still clinging to hope for a deal, even though it still seems quite a gap between us and Iran at the moment. But that hope is, I think, the only thing stopping oil, maybe getting back to $100 at the moment.
